title: Pharmacology, adverse reactions and polypharmacy
blurb: Recognise side effects, allergies and interactions, report suspected reactions on Yellow Card, and support medication review in polypharmacy.
question: A woman started a new medicine marked with a black triangle two weeks ago and now has a mild itchy rash. Should the nurse report it on the Yellow Card scheme?

teach.body: Pharmacodynamics is what a drug does to the body; pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion). A side effect is a known effect other than the one intended, such as a dry cough with ACE inhibitors. An adverse drug reaction (ADR) is a harmful, unintended response. An allergy is an immune reaction, which can be life-threatening. Nurses must know each medicine's effects, side effects, contraindications and interactions before giving it.

rows.label: Timing
values: Immediate: usually within 1 hour; delayed rashes days later
Related to dose or known effect

values: Drug allergy: drug, reaction and severity, date

teach.caption: CG183: a reaction is less likely to be allergy if it is gastrointestinal symptoms alone or has a possible non-drug cause.

items: Record one of: 'drug allergy', 'none known' or 'unable to ascertain', as soon as the information is available.
If allergy: record the drug name, the signs, symptoms and severity, and the date it occurred.
For a new suspected reaction: drug (generic and brand, strength, form), description, indication, date and time, doses before onset, route, and what to avoid in future.
Check allergy status against every prescription before administration.

teach.caption: Code 18.3: check compatibility of what you give with other medicines, including over-the-counter medicines.
You do not need to prove the medicine caused it: suspicion is enough. Anyone, including patients and carers, can report to the MHRA.

teach.body: People taking multiple medicines, those with long-term conditions and older people may benefit from a structured medication review with a clear purpose (NICE NG5 1.4.1). Falls, confusion or new symptoms in someone on many medicines should prompt the question: could this be a medicine? Reconciliation on admission lists all medicines, including over-the-counter and complementary products, within 24 hours in acute care (NG5 1.3.1). Ask specifically about herbal remedies, which people often do not think of as medicines.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Ade and Derek
teach.body: On admission Derek, 59, says he is 'allergic to codeine'. Ade asks what happened: it made him nauseous and constipated, with no rash, swelling or breathing problems. These are gastrointestinal effects, which CG183 says make allergy less likely, so Ade records a codeine intolerance with the specific effects rather than a drug allergy. He also learns Derek takes St John's wort, records it and tells the prescriber because it interacts with several medicines, including warfarin.

teach.caption: RPS/RCN 18: ADRs are managed under policy, documented and reported nationally (Yellow Card) or locally.

teach.text: Not every bad experience is an allergy. Nausea or constipation from codeine is an intolerance; labelling it 'allergy' may deny the person useful medicines in future. But never dismiss urticaria, swelling, wheeze or low blood pressure: those suggest true allergy.

items: Know effects, side effects, contraindications and interactions before giving a medicine.
Allergy status: 'drug allergy', 'none known' or 'unable to ascertain'; record drug, reaction, severity, date.
Yellow Card: all suspected ADRs for ▼ medicines; serious ones for established medicines; suspicion is enough.
Ask about over-the-counter and herbal products: St John's wort reduces warfarin's effect; ibuprofen adds bleeding risk.
Polypharmacy, long-term conditions and older age: consider a structured medication review.

summary: You can now tell side effects, intolerance and allergy apart, document allergy status to NICE CG183 and recognise key interactions. You can also decide when to make a Yellow Card report and when to request a medication review.

A.q: Shona, 44, started a new medicine marked with a black triangle (▼) two weeks ago. She now has a mild itchy rash and no other symptoms. What should the nurse do about reporting?
options: Report it on Yellow Card, as all suspected ▼ reactions are reported
Report it if the rash becomes severe or she needs admission to hospital
Report it once the prescriber has proved the medicine caused it
Do not report it, as rashes are listed in the patient leaflet
A.why: The MHRA asks healthcare professionals to report all suspected ADRs to black triangle medicines; a suspicion is enough and causality need not be proven.

whyNot.1: The 'serious only' threshold applies to established medicines, not ▼ medicines.
whyNot.2: Proof of causality is not required; suspicion is enough.
whyNot.3: Being listed does not remove the request to report all suspected reactions to ▼ medicines.

A.q: On admission, Derek, 59, says he is 'allergic' to codeine. When asked, he explains it made him nauseated and constipated, with no rash, swelling or breathing problems. How should this be recorded?
options: As a codeine allergy, as he describes it that way
As 'unable to ascertain' until formal allergy testing has been done
As 'none known', as these are normal side effects
As a codeine intolerance, noting nausea and constipation
A.why: Gastrointestinal symptoms alone make drug allergy less likely (CG183 1.1.3). Recording the specific intolerance keeps information accurate without wrongly labelling an allergy.

whyNot.0: His description fits known side effects, not an immune reaction.
whyNot.1: The history is clear enough to record; 'unable to ascertain' is for when information cannot be obtained.
whyNot.2: The reaction should be recorded so prescribers know about it.

A.q: Maureen, 66, started ramipril 6 weeks ago. She tells the community nurse she has had a persistent dry, tickly cough since, with no fever. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Advise her to stop the ramipril today and to see the GP next month
Reassure her it is viral and will settle within a week
Explain cough is a known ramipril effect and arrange a review
Advise an over-the-counter cough linctus and continue
A.why: Cough is a common side effect of ACE inhibitors such as ramipril (BNF). The prescriber should review, as an alternative may be considered.

whyNot.0: Stopping an antihypertensive without prescriber advice may be unsafe, and review should not wait a month.
whyNot.1: A 6-week cough starting with ramipril is more likely a drug effect than a virus.
whyNot.3: Masking the cough with linctus misses the cause.

B.q: Bill, 71, takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation and has a stable INR. He tells the practice nurse he plans to buy ibuprofen for knee pain. What is the best advice?
options: Avoid ibuprofen, and discuss safer options with the pharmacist or GP
Ibuprofen is fine for short-term use at the usual over-the-counter dose
Take ibuprofen, but halve his own warfarin dose for that week
Take ibuprofen with food to protect his stomach
B.why: Warfarin and ibuprofen both increase bleeding risk; the BNF rates the interaction as severe. He should avoid ibuprofen and seek advice on alternatives.

whyNot.1: Short courses still carry the added bleeding risk.
whyNot.2: Changing warfarin doses without a prescriber is unsafe.
whyNot.3: Food does not remove the bleeding interaction.

B.q: Cyril, 82, has heart failure and takes IV furosemide and digoxin. His morning potassium is 3.1 mmol/L, down from 4.0. He feels well. What should the nurse do?
options: Recheck the potassium next week when his routine bloods are due
Encourage a banana at lunch and continue all medicines as prescribed
Ask for an extra dose of IV furosemide to protect his heart from overload
Inform the prescriber now, as low potassium is dangerous with digoxin
B.why: Loop diuretics cause hypokalaemia, which the BNF notes is dangerous in patients also taking cardiac glycosides such as digoxin. The prescriber needs to know promptly.

whyNot.1: Diet alone is not an adequate response to a falling potassium on digoxin.
whyNot.2: More furosemide would lower his potassium further.

B.q: Five minutes into an IV antibiotic infusion, Graham, 60, develops a hoarse voice, wheeze, widespread urticaria and a blood pressure of 78/40. What should the nurse do first?
options: Slow the infusion rate right down and recheck his observations in 15 minutes
Stop the infusion, call for help and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Give oral chlorphenamine and continue the infusion
Complete a Yellow Card report before treating
B.why: These are airway, breathing and circulation problems with skin changes: anaphylaxis. Remove the trigger, call for help and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (1 mg/mL) for an adult (RCUK).

whyNot.0: Slowing the infusion continues exposure and delays treatment.
whyNot.2: Antihistamines are third-line and not for ABC problems; the infusion must stop.

C.q: Gemma, 35, lists citalopram as her only regular medicine. When asked about other products, she says she has been taking St John's wort for a month. What should the nurse do?
options: Leave it unrecorded, as herbal products are not classed as medicines
Remove it from her locker without discussion
Tell her to double her citalopram instead
Record it and inform the prescriber, as it can interact
C.why: Reconciliation includes over-the-counter and complementary medicines (NG5 1.3.1). St John's wort interacts with a number of medicines, so the prescriber must know (Code 18.3).

whyNot.0: Herbal products can have significant interactions and must be recorded.
whyNot.1: Removing her property without discussion breaches her autonomy and does not inform the prescriber.
whyNot.2: Changing a prescribed dose is not the nurse's decision and does not address the interaction.

C.q: Winifred, 86, lives alone and takes 12 regular medicines from three prescribers. She has fallen twice this month and her daughter reports increasing drowsiness. What is the most appropriate action for the community nurse?
options: Advise her to stop the medicines that she feels are the least important
Request a structured medication review with her GP and pharmacist
Arrange a falls alarm and continue all medicines unchanged
Increase her fluid intake and review her in 3 months
C.why: Polypharmacy with falls and drowsiness suggests possible medicine-related harm; NICE NG5 recommends considering a structured medication review for people on multiple medicines and older people.

whyNot.0: Stopping medicines without review may cause withdrawal or loss of control of conditions.
whyNot.2: An alarm does not address the likely cause.

C.q: A nurse checks the allergy status of Mr Ruiz on admission. He is unconscious and has no relatives present or records available. How should his allergy status be documented?
options: 'Unable to ascertain', updated when known
'None known', as no allergy has been reported
Leave the section blank until he wakes
'Penicillin allergy' as a precaution
C.why: CG183 1.2.1: document drug allergy status using 'drug allergy', 'none known' or 'unable to ascertain', as soon as the information is available.

whyNot.1: 'None known' implies the question was asked and answered; it has not been.
whyNot.2: A blank section may be read as 'checked and none', which is unsafe.
whyNot.3: Inventing an allergy is inaccurate and may deny useful treatment.

reteach.title: Ask 'could this be the medicine?'
reteach.question: When a person develops a new problem, how often is a medicine the cause?

blocks.body: Falls, confusion, rashes, a cough or a low potassium can all be caused by medicines. The safest habit is to ask: what changed recently, what are they taking (including from the shop and herbal remedies), and does this fit a known effect or interaction? Then tell the prescriber, record it properly, and report suspected reactions.

blocks.text: Yellow Card is for suspicion, not proof. For ▼ medicines report everything; for established medicines report serious reactions.

explain.body: Known effects other than the intended one, such as cough with ACE inhibitors or hypokalaemia with loop diuretics. Monitor, report and review.

test.q: Which electrolyte disturbance is a recognised effect of loop diuretics such as furosemide?
options: Hyperkalaemia
Hypernatraemia
Hypercalcaemia
Hypokalaemia
test.why: BNF: hypokalaemia can occur with loop diuretics, and electrolytes are monitored during treatment.

whyNot.0: Loop diuretics increase potassium loss rather than causing a raised potassium.
whyNot.1: Raised sodium is not the classic loop diuretic disturbance.
whyNot.2: Raised calcium is not the characteristic loop diuretic effect.

explain.body: Status: drug allergy, none known or unable to ascertain. Record drug, signs and severity, and date. GI symptoms alone make allergy less likely.

test.q: According to NICE CG183, which feature makes a reaction less likely to be a drug allergy?
options: Gastrointestinal symptoms alone
Urticaria within an hour of the dose
Swelling of the lips and tongue
Wheeze and low blood pressure
test.why: CG183 1.1.3: a reaction is less likely to be drug allergy if the person has gastrointestinal symptoms only or there is a possible non-drug cause.

whyNot.1: Urticaria within an hour suggests an immediate allergic reaction.

explain.body: Warfarin with ibuprofen: more bleeding. Warfarin with St John's wort: less anticoagulant effect. Low potassium with digoxin: greater danger. Always ask about shop-bought and herbal products.

test.q: What effect does St John's wort have on warfarin, according to the BNF?
options: It increases the anticoagulant effect
It has no recognised interaction
It decreases the anticoagulant effect
It causes warfarin to be excreted unchanged
test.why: BNF: St John's wort decreases the anticoagulant effect of warfarin; the manufacturer advises avoiding the combination.

whyNot.0: The interaction reduces, rather than increases, the effect.
whyNot.1: The BNF does list an interaction, and the combination is to be avoided.
whyNot.3: This is not the described mechanism or effect.

explain.body: MHRA scheme for suspected ADRs and problems with medicines, vaccines, devices and more. Report all suspected ADRs for ▼ medicines and serious ones for established medicines. Anyone can report.

test.q: Who can submit a Yellow Card report to the MHRA?
options: Doctors and pharmacists
Any registered healthcare professional in the UK
Anyone, including patients and carers
The manufacturer of the medicine
test.why: The Yellow Card site states anyone can report an issue with a medicine, vaccine, device, blood product or e-cigarette.

whyNot.0: Reporting is not restricted to doctors and pharmacists.
whyNot.1: Patients and the public can also report.
whyNot.3: Manufacturers have their own duties, but the scheme is open to everyone.
